How to Verify a Contractor's Business License and Protect Your Investment

Protect your home improvement project by verifying your contractor's license, insurance, and complaint history before signing any contract.

Key takeaways

  • ✓Verify the license on the state licensing board website and confirm it is active and covers your type of work.
  • ✓A license does not prove quality or insurance, so ask for proof of insurance directly from the insurer.
  • ✓Check court records and complaint history before signing.

Why License Verification is Crucial

Hiring an unlicensed or improperly credentialed contractor is one of the riskiest decisions a homeowner or business owner can make. It can lead to substandard, unsafe work, massive financial loss, and severe legal liability. For example, if an unlicensed worker is injured on your property and lacks proper workers' compensation insurance, you could be held personally responsible for their medical bills and lost wages. Verifying a contractor's license ensures they have met the state's minimum standards for competency, financial responsibility, bonding, and legal compliance.

Step 1: Check the State Licensing Board

Every state has a dedicated contractor licensing board, often operating under the Department of Consumer Affairs, Department of Professional Regulation, or a similar regulatory agency. Their official website will feature a "License Check," "Contractor Lookup," or "Verify a License" tool. To use it, you will need either the contractor's exact legal business name or their specific license number. A reputable contractor will provide this number willingly and prominently on their estimates, business cards, and website.

Step 2: Review the License Details Carefully

Once you locate the license in the state database, do not just check if it exists. You must verify the following critical details:

  • Current Status: Ensure the license is explicitly listed as "Active," "Current," or "In Good Standing." An "Expired," "Suspended," or "Revoked" status is an immediate, non-negotiable red flag.
  • License Classification: Ensure the license specifically covers the type of work you are having done. A "General Building Contractor" license may not legally cover specialized electrical, plumbing, or HVAC work, which often requires separate, specialized trade licenses.
  • Bonding and Insurance: Many state portals will indicate whether the contractor has an active contractor's bond and general liability insurance on file. This is your financial safety net if the job goes wrong.
  • Expiration Date: Confirm the license is valid and won't expire midway through your projected project timeline.

Step 3: Check for Complaints and Disciplinary Actions

The state licensing board's portal will also display the contractor's official disciplinary history. Look for any formal consumer complaints, citations, administrative fines, or past license suspensions. A clean record is a strong indicator of a reputable, professional business. If you see a pattern of multiple unresolved complaints, especially regarding abandoned jobs or poor workmanship, walk away immediately and find another contractor.

Step 4: Cross-Reference with the Better Business Bureau (BBB)

While the state board handles legal licensing, the local Better Business Bureau (BBB) is an excellent resource for checking informal customer reviews and dispute resolution history. A contractor with an "A+" rating and a history of resolving customer complaints professionally is generally a safe bet. Always get at least three written, detailed estimates before making your final decision.

What a License Does and Does Not Prove

An active license shows that the contractor met the state's requirements to work in a particular trade and classification. It does not guarantee quality, honesty, or financial stability. Check that the license class covers the type of work you are hiring for, since many states have separate classifications for different trades or project sizes. Also confirm that the name on the license matches the name on the contract and the person who will sign it.

Insurance and Bonds

  • General liability insurance: covers property damage or injuries caused by the work.
  • Workers' compensation: covers injuries to the contractor's employees. If it is missing, you could face risk if a worker is hurt on your property, depending on your state's rules.
  • License bond: some states require a bond that can compensate customers in certain cases.

Ask for a certificate of insurance and request that it be sent directly from the insurer or agent rather than relying on a copy from the contractor. Confirm the policy dates are current.

Risks of Hiring an Unlicensed Contractor

Rules differ, but in some states an unlicensed contractor cannot enforce a payment contract in court, and homeowners may lose access to certain protections or recovery funds. Local permits can also be a problem, because many jurisdictions require a licensed contractor to pull permits for larger jobs. If a contractor asks you to pull permits yourself or pay mostly in cash, ask why.

Verification Checklist

  • Look up the license number on the state licensing board site.
  • Confirm status is active and the expiration date is in the future.
  • Check the classification matches the job.
  • Read any complaints, citations, or disciplinary actions.
  • Search county court records for lawsuits involving the contractor.
  • Verify insurance directly with the provider.
  • Get a written contract and a payment schedule tied to progress.
